product.title: Swedish 102 - A2 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from A1 to a solid A2 in Swedish. Dian's second year in Stockholm — a shared flat on Södermalm, a part-time job at a café, evening classes, a first visit to the doctor, a first Midsommar — gives you everyday dialogues with word-for-word translations, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises and an answer key. The units go straight at the spots that trip A2 learners up: particle verbs with the stress on the little word, verbs ending in -s, the s-passive, inte moving in front of the verb in subordinate clauses, tycka/tro/tänka, i/på/om/för … sedan with time, hem vs hemma, and the small words ju, väl and nog.

blocks.text: Welcome back. If you have worked through **Svenska 101**, you can already do a surprising amount in Swedish: introduce yourself, order a *kanelbulle*, ask the way, tell the time, say what you did yesterday, and build a sentence with the verb firmly in second place. That is A1. What you can't do yet is keep a conversation going — tell a longer story, explain *why*, say what you would do *if*, or report what somebody else said. That is what A2 is for.

A2 is the level of **everyday life**. Not the tourist's Swedish of A1, but the Swedish of someone who lives here: signing a lease, starting a job, calling the health center, complaining politely about a late delivery, chatting with the regulars at work. The vocabulary roughly doubles, and the sentences get longer, because real life is full of *when*, *because*, *before*, *although* and *if*.

The good news first. Most of what is new at A2 has a close English cousin. **Particle verbs** — *ta på sig*, *stänga av*, *komma ihåg* — work just like *put on*, *turn off* and *give up*. The **s-passive** (*Kaffet serveras klockan åtta*, "Coffee is served at eight") is one ending instead of a two-word construction. *Om jag vann skulle jag …* is word for word "If I won, I would …". You will often feel that Swedish is simply English with the furniture moved around.

Now the hard parts, named up front so they don't ambush you. There are four: **the stress in particle verbs** (in *tycka OM* the little word carries the stress — get it wrong and you may say a different verb); **verbs ending in -s**, which can be passive (*öppnas*), reciprocal (*vi ses*) or neither (*hoppas*, *finnas*); **word order in subordinate clauses**, where *inte* jumps in front of the verb (*… att hon inte kom*) and questions lose their inversion (*Hon frågade var jag bor*); and **three verbs for one English "think"** — *tycka*, *tro* and *tänka*. Each gets its own unit, and each comes back again and again.

The story picks up where Svenska 101 ended. It is **Dian**'s second year in Stockholm. She leaves the Lappis corridor and moves into a shared flat on Södermalm with **Elin** and Elin's younger brother **Jonas**, who plays in a band. She finds a part-time job at a café run by **Maja**, takes evening classes with a teacher called **Lena**, still sees **Oskar** and **Ahmad**, catches her first Swedish cold, and ends the year at a Midsommar celebration in Dalarna with Elin's parents, **Anna** and **Lars**.

Twenty units again, one dialogue each, but a little longer and a little faster than before — plan on thirty to forty minutes per sitting. One unit every two or three days gets you to the last page in about two months. *Lycka till!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit builds on Svenska 101 and on the units before it.

blocks.text: Like Svenska 101, this course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, now about 30-40 minutes. What matters is still not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout as before:

items: **Dialogue** — read the Swedish out loud first, without the translation. At A2 the dialogues are longer and closer to real speech, with interruptions, small talk and little words like *ju* and *väl*. Read each one at least twice: once for the story, once for the details.

**Literal translation** — the italic line under the translation. Keep reading it. At this level it shows you the things that matter most: where the particle sits in *ta på sig*, where *inte* goes in a subordinate clause, and what an *-s* ending is doing.
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt strange, with pronunciation tips where the spelling misleads you.
**Grammar** — one to three short sections per unit, each with a table you can come back to.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit. Nouns always come with *en* or *ett*; verbs that are strong or irregular are worth saying aloud in all their forms.
**Exercises** — word-order puzzles, fill-ins and translations. Do them without looking at the key, and say your answers out loud.
**Answer key** — open it only after you have genuinely tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: Every unit points you back to an earlier one — Unit 1 points back to Svenska 101, and the rest to earlier units of this book. Do it in reverse: cover the Swedish, read the English translation, and rebuild the Swedish from memory. Then check.
A2 is where many learners stall, because they keep moving forward and never let anything settle. The wave review is the cure. Don't skip it.

blocks.title: Make it your own
items: After each dialogue, write three sentences about your own life using the new grammar: your weekend, your home, your job, what you would do if you won the lottery. Words you use about yourself stick far better than words you only read.
Read the dialogue aloud once more a week later. You will be surprised how much faster it goes.

blocks.text: And the rule that never changes: **say it out loud**. The "Say it" column uses the same respelling system as Svenska 101 — capital letters mark the stressed syllable, **ü** is Swedish *u*, **hw** is the *sj*-sound. If a respelling ever puzzles you, the pronunciation chapter of Svenska 101 has the full key; the short refresher on the next pages covers what is new at A2.

You know the sounds of Swedish from Svenska 101. At A2 the challenge moves from single words to **whole sentences**: how they rise and fall, which words get squeezed, and which words carry the weight. Read this once now and come back to it whenever natural speech seems too fast.
Sentence melody: one peak per phrase

In a Swedish sentence, not every word is stressed. The words that carry new information — nouns, main verbs, adjectives, and the particle in a particle verb — get the stress. The little words around them — pronouns, *en/ett*, *är*, *har*, most prepositions — are said quickly and lightly. The most important word of the phrase (the **focus**) gets the highest peak, and statements end low: *Jag har köpt en ny CYKEL.*

Yes/no questions are marked by word order (*Har du ätit?*), so they don't need to rise at the end the way English questions often do. A Swedish question can sound flat or even falling to English ears — that is normal, not rude.

blocks.title: Particle verbs: stress the little word
items: In a particle verb, the particle takes the stress and the verb goes light: *tycka om* → **tük-kah OM**, *stänga av* → **steng-ah AHV**, *komma ihåg* → **kom-mah i-HOHG**.

With an ordinary preposition, it is the other way around: *titta på tv* → **TIT-tah poh** … The verb is stressed and *på* is light. Stress is often the only thing that tells you which kind of word you are hearing.

blocks.text: The two tones, once more

Tone 1 is a single fall; tone 2 falls, then rises again, and gives Swedish its sing-song sound. Most native words of two syllables have tone 2 (*flicka*, *gata*, *springa*). Two habits help at A2: a one-syllable noun **keeps tone 1** when it gets the definite ending (*bil* → *bilen*, *hus* → *huset*), and **compound words always get tone 2**, with a second, weaker stress on the last part (*SOMmar·stugan*, *VÅRD·centralen*). That is why *tanken* ("the tank", tone 1) and *tanken* ("the thought", tone 2) can sound different — but context will rescue you every time.
What Swedes actually say

In ordinary speech, several very common words lose letters. You will hear these short forms constantly, and you will see many of them in texts, chat messages and song lyrics. You don't have to use them yourself, but you must recognize them.

blocks.text: *Sa*, *la*, *sen*, *ska* and *dom* are so common that many Swedes also write them in everyday texts. In careful writing, though, stick to *de/dem*, *sedan*, *något* and *mig/dig/sig*.

blocks.title: Two word-order rules that never take a day off
items: **Inside** a subordinate clause, *inte* and other sentence adverbs come **before** the verb: *… eftersom hon **inte kom***, *… att jag **aldrig har** varit där*.
When a subordinate clause comes **first**, it counts as one element, and the main verb comes right after it: *När jag kom hem, **åt** jag.* — never *När jag kom hem, jag åt*.

What the -s does

blocks.text: In the present, *-er* verbs simply drop the *-er* before adding *-s*: *stänger* → *stängs*, *säljer* → *säljs*.
bli and vara + participle (Unit 6)

*Vara* describes a state, *bli* a change or an event: *Dörren **är** stängd.* (it is closed) · *Vi **blev** inbjudna.* (we got invited). The participle agrees with the subject like any adjective: *Affären är stängd. Fönstret är stängt. Affärerna är stängda.*
Reflexive verbs (Unit 7)
Why and so (Unit 8)

head: Word
Use
Example
rows: because, since — subordinate clause, can come first
*Vi stannade hemma därför att det regnade.*
that's why — main clause, verb second
so — joins two main clauses; keep normal word order after it (*så vi*, not *så stannade vi*)

blocks.text: Adjectives: the special ones (Unit 9)

After a possessive (*min, Elins*), the adjective takes *-a* but the noun has **no** definite ending: *min nya cykel*, not *min nya cykeln*. After *den här / det där*, both get the ending: *den här nya cykeln*. *Hela* and *halva* take the definite noun: *hela dagen*, *halva tiden*.

*fort – fortare – fortast*, *ofta – oftare – oftast*, *gärna – hellre – helst*

blocks.text: Should, need, get to (Units 11 and 18)
The trap: **får inte** means "must not", while *måste inte* means "don't have to". For "don't have to", say **behöver inte** — that way you never risk being misunderstood.

blocks.text: Talking about the future: **ska** for plans and decisions (*Jag ska jobba i kväll*), **kommer att** for predictions (*Det kommer att regna*), **tänker** for intentions (*Jag tänker säga upp mig*).

blocks.text: Reported questions keep statement word order — subject before verb, *inte* before the verb. When the question word is the subject, add **som**. If what was said is still true, keep the present tense; Swedes also often shift to the past (*Hon sa att hon var trött*) — the full tense shift comes in Svenska 103.

blocks.text: Particle verbs are the backbone of everyday Swedish, and Unit 3 is only the beginning — you will meet them in every unit after it. Here are sixty of the most useful, grouped roughly by particle. Remember the two rules: **the particle is stressed** (*tycka OM*, *stänga AV*), and **the object comes after the particle** — even a short pronoun: *Stäng av den*, *Stäng av mobilen*, *Ta på dig jackan*. Sentence adverbs like *inte* go between verb and particle: *Jag tycker inte om fisk*.

head: Particle verb
Meaning
Example
rows: *Kan du ta upp det på mötet?*
*Vad ska du ha på dig i kväll?*

blocks.title: How to learn them
items: Don't learn the list from top to bottom. Pick the five verbs you need this week and use them in a sentence about your own life, out loud.

Notice the patterns: *upp* often means "finished" or "up" (*äta upp*, *växa upp*), *av* often means "off" (*stänga av*, *stiga av*), *med* often means "along" (*följa med*, *ta med*), *tillbaka* always means "back".

blocks.text: You have reached the end of A2. You can now tell the story of your weekend, explain why you did something, say what you would do if, report what someone said, deal with a doctor's appointment or a landlord, and write a polite email. Swedes will start answering you in Swedish more often — and you will understand more of their answer than you think.
Three things waiting for you at B1

items: **Three layers of the past.** *Jag hade redan ätit när hon kom* — "I had already eaten when she came." The pluperfect lets you tell a story in the right order, and B1 puts it to work from the very first unit.

**Strong verbs as families.** *skriva – skrev – skrivit*, *dricka – drack – druckit*, *flyga – flög – flugit*. Instead of learning them one by one, you will learn them in vowel families, the way Swedish children absorb them.

**Swedish at work.** Dian moves to Göteborg for an internship. Meetings, *fika* with colleagues, the Swedish love of consensus, Skatteverket and the *personnummer*, and, at the end, a real job application.

blocks.text: Habits that help more than the next book

items: **Listen to *Klartext*.** Sveriges Radio's daily news in easy Swedish is the perfect A2 listening practice: real news, slow and clear, a few minutes a day. *8 Sidor* is its written counterpart.
**Keep watching with Swedish subtitles.** At A2, try shows made for adults — drama, cooking, reality TV — rather than children's programs. Pause, repeat a line, carry on.
**Write a short diary.** Five sentences every evening, in the past tense: what you did, why, and what you think about it. You will use exactly the grammar of this book.
**Find one Swedish speaker you see every week.** A *språkcafé*, a colleague, a neighbor, an online tandem partner. Regular, short conversations beat occasional long ones.

blocks.title: A note about the in-between stage
items: Somewhere around A2 most learners hit a plateau: you understand a lot, but speaking still feels slow. That is normal, and it is a sign that your understanding has run ahead of your speaking — which is exactly the right order.
The way through is not more grammar, but more **talking**. Say the dialogues aloud, describe your day aloud, and keep using your lifesaver: **"Kan vi prata svenska? Jag övar."**

blocks.text: *Tack för att du har följt med Dian hela vägen hit. Vi ses i Göteborg!* — Thanks for coming along with Dian all the way here. See you in Göteborg!
